lessons.title: Table-driven tests
lessons.summary: If the above row expects 11 instead of 10, what happens?
explanation: A table-driven test stores named inputs and expected results in a slice of struct values. Here []struct declares a slice whose element type is an anonymous structure; each row fills name, input and want in order. The same assertion runs for every row.

Save this complete example as main_test.go in a local module and run go test -run TestClamp -v. t.Run names each subtest; its callback receives that subtest’s *testing.T. t.Fatalf reports the actual and wanted values and ends the failing subtest. PASS and timing lines come from the test runner, not a hardcoded program print.
Expected output or behavior: All three named subtests PASS; runner timings vary. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Context and cancellation
lessons.summary: If cancel is called twice before waiting, what prints?
explanation: context.WithCancel derives a cancellable context and returns a CancelFunc. The notation <-ctx.Done() receives from that channel, waiting until cancellation closes it; channel operations are developed in the following lessons. Calling cancel closes the context’s Done channel; it does not forcibly terminate arbitrary code. Operations must observe cancellation and stop cooperatively.

Defer cancel even when another branch may cancel earlier; repeated calls are safe. After cancellation, Err reports context.Canceled. Background has no deadline and is a root context, not an automatic timeout. This fixture cancels immediately without waiting for a timer.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
"context"
)


func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    cancel()
    <-ctx.Done()
    fmt.Println(ctx.Err() == context.Canceled)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why returning a cancel function creates an ownership obligation even when no timeout is used. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Goroutines and completion
lessons.summary: If the worker assigns 11, what prints after receiving from done?
explanation: go invokes a function concurrently with its caller. The func() { ... }() form declares and immediately invokes an anonymous function; go changes that invocation into a goroutine. main does not automatically wait for every goroutine before the program exits.

make(chan struct{}) creates an unbuffered channel carrying empty-struct signals. The worker writes result and closes done. Receiving from the closed channel unblocks main; that synchronization orders the preceding write before the read. Only the worker owns closing done, and no sleep guesses are involved.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
)


func main() {
    done := make(chan struct{})
    result := 0
    go func() { result = 7; close(done) }()
    <-done
    fmt.Println(result)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Unbuffered channels
lessons.summary: If the worker sends 8 instead, what prints?
explanation: make(chan int) creates an unbuffered channel. A send ch <- value and a receive <-ch rendezvous; the sender cannot finish the send until a receiver is ready. Channels communicate typed values, not arbitrary shared memory transactions.

The worker sends one integer, then closes a separate completion channel. main receives the value and waits for done so the worker’s lifetime is complete before returning. Closing the data channel is unnecessary when the receiver knows exactly one value is expected.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
)


func main() {
    values := make(chan int)
    done := make(chan struct{})
    go func() { values <- 6; close(done) }()
    value := <-values
    <-done
    fmt.Println(value * 2)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: WaitGroup lifecycle
lessons.summary: If the worker stores 11, what prints after Wait?
explanation: sync.WaitGroup tracks outstanding tasks. Add(1) runs before launching the goroutine; the worker defers Done so its task count decreases when it returns. Wait blocks until the count reaches zero. Do not copy a WaitGroup after first use.

WaitGroup coordinates lifetime, not arbitrary simultaneous writes. This example has one worker writing result and main reads only after Wait, so there is no competing access. Adding concurrent writers would require a separate synchronization policy.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
"sync"
)


func main() {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    result := 0
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); result = 7 }()
    wg.Wait()
    fmt.Println(result)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Mutex-protected state
lessons.summary: If each worker increments 25 times, what is the final count?
explanation: count++ is not atomic. Every concurrent update here locks the same sync.Mutex, changes count and unlocks it. A mutex’s zero value is usable; never copy it after use. Different mutex objects would not protect this one shared counter.

Two workers each make 100 protected increments. WaitGroup counts both before launch and each worker defers Done. After Wait, neither worker accesses count again, so the final observation is safe. The fixture does not run an intentionally racy unlocked variant.
Expected output or behavior: 200. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Atomic counters
lessons.summary: If each update adds 2 instead of 1, what prints?
explanation: atomic.Int64 provides Add and Load operations on an integer. Its zero value starts at zero, and Add returns the new value. Do not copy an atomic object after first use. Atomic operations have sequentially consistent ordering, not a promise about a particular implementation speed.

Two workers update the same typed atomic and finish before Load. This avoids lost increments for the one counter. Combining several separate Load and Store calls would not automatically make an entire algorithm atomic or preserve an invariant involving other fields.

lessons.title: Cancellation-aware worker lifetime
lessons.summary: If cancellation happens before starting the goroutine instead, what prints after done?
explanation: Cancellation alone does not wait for a goroutine to exit. This owner supplies a context, cancels it and then waits for a separate done channel. The worker owns closing done using defer, so main returns only after cleanup and result assignment.

The worker receives from ctx.Done; if cancellation already happened, that receive is immediately ready. This handles both cancellation before start and cancellation while waiting without a timing assumption. A worker doing other blocking work would also need cancellation-aware operations at those boundaries.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
"context"
)


func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    done := make(chan struct{})
    result := "waiting"
    go func() {
        defer close(done)
        <-ctx.Done()
        result = "stopped"
    }()
    cancel()
    <-done
    fmt.Println(result)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: stopped. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: HTTP handler contracts
lessons.summary: If the request method becomes POST, what status and body result?
explanation: An HTTP handler receives an http.ResponseWriter and *http.Request. Set headers before WriteHeader or the first body write; the first body write would otherwise imply status 200. Once headers are committed, later header edits generally cannot change the response already sent.

httptest.NewRequest constructs an in-memory incoming request, and NewRecorder records handler output. Calling handler directly performs no HTTP network request. This example accepts GET and returns a 405 rejection with an Allow: GET header for other methods; fmt.Fprint’s write error is checked, although the in-memory recorder does not simulate a broken network connection.

lessons.title: HTTP client deadlines and transport
lessons.summary: If the context deadline is already in the past, what does this fake transaction report?
explanation: http.Client delegates a single transaction to its RoundTripper. This fake transport returns an in-memory response and never calls the default transport, DNS, a listener or a socket. io.NopCloser wraps the strings.Reader with a Close method that does nothing; it does not acquire or release an external resource. Its RoundTrip checks the request context. Real custom transports must also honor cancellation during their actual blocking work.

NewRequestWithContext attaches the context; a one-hour timeout here is a bound, not a timing assertion. Defer cancel releases context resources. On successful Do, close the response body even when reading fails. A received HTTP error status is not automatically a Do transport error; inspect StatusCode separately. The fixture reads only its known tiny in-memory body.
Expected output or behavior: 200 ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: A bounded study pipeline
lessons.summary: If the first input changes from 15 to 70, what is the total?
explanation: This producer considers a fixed list of minute counts. It sends only values 1 through 60, choosing to skip invalid inputs rather than convert them to zero. The send-only chan<- int parameter documents that the producer sends and closes but does not receive.

The producer defers closing the values channel and a completion channel. The consumer ranges until values is closed, then waits for done before printing its total. A fixed source bounds this exercise; a consumer that exits early would need a cancellation-aware send so the producer cannot remain blocked. No early-exit consumer is used here.
Expected output or behavior: 35. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
